title: Coinbase Earnings Beat Estimates With Surprise $718.7 Million Profit as Crypto Gains Offset a 35% Revenue Drop
excerpt: Coinbase's $2.51 EPS crushed forecasts of a loss, but $715 million of the profit was an unrealized crypto gain; adjusted net income fell to $77.7 million as trading revenue dropped 44%.
body:
• Coinbase posted a surprise third-quarter profit: net income of $718.7 million, or $2.51 per diluted share, against analyst forecasts of a loss — but $715 million of it was an unrealized gain on crypto the company holds for investment.
  • Revenue fell 35% year over year to $1.22 billion, roughly in line with consensus, as transaction revenue dropped 44% to $590 million on much weaker spot trading; subscription and services revenue was $570 million, 49% of net revenue.
  • Adjusted net income was just $77.7 million, down from $420.7 million a year ago, and operating income fell to $61.7 million; adjusted EBITDA of $332.9 million still beat estimates and stayed positive for a 15th straight quarter.
  • Prediction markets, launched in January, now run at $200 million of annualized revenue, and Coinbase guided fourth-quarter subscription and services revenue to $550 million–$630 million.

Coinbase Global swung to a surprise profit in the third quarter of 2026, the company reported Thursday after the close in its quarterly filing with the SEC, even as the underlying trading business shrank sharply with the crypto market. Net income rose 66% from a year earlier to $718.7 million, or $2.51 per diluted share, up from $1.50 a year ago and far ahead of forecasts that centered on a small loss — FactSet analysts had penciled in a loss of 23 cents per share.

A profit built on a crypto rebound

The headline number flatters the operating business. Nearly all of the profit came from a $715 million unrealized gain on crypto assets Coinbase holds as an investment, which rose in value as bitcoin climbed 39% during the quarter ended September 30. Strip that out and adjusted net income was $77.7 million, down from $420.7 million in the same quarter last year. Operating income — the profit from actually running the exchange — fell to $61.7 million from $480.5 million a year earlier.

Total revenue fell 35% year over year to $1.22 billion, roughly flat from the second quarter and essentially in line with consensus estimates clustered around $1.21 billion to $1.23 billion. Transaction revenue dropped 44% to $590 million, though that still beat the roughly $527 million analysts expected, and total operating expenses fell 13% from the prior quarter to $1.154 billion. Adjusted EBITDA was $332.9 million, ahead of the $290.2 million consensus, and Coinbase ended the quarter with $8.6 billion of cash and cash equivalents.

Trading shrinks, steadier lines grow

Spot trading volume was about $134.5 billion, roughly half of last year's level, as retail activity cooled alongside prices — bitcoin traded near $80,400 this week, down from above $122,000 last October. Coinbase nevertheless took a bigger share of a smaller market: its share of spot volume rose to 10.7% from 5.6% a year ago, as CoinCentral's coverage of the report noted.

The offset came from businesses that do not depend on trading. Subscription and services revenue rose 3% from the second quarter to $570 million — down 20% from a year ago, but now 49% of net revenue against 41% last year. Stablecoin-related revenue accounted for $307 million of that total, and average USDC balances held in Coinbase products hit a record $22 billion, up 49% year over year, for a 14th consecutive record quarter. Prediction markets, launched in January, now generate $200 million in annualized revenue, growing at an 82% compound quarterly rate, with trader numbers up 60% from the second quarter.

“Better than feared.”

— Dan Dolev, Mizuho analyst, on the quarter

Investors focused on the softer core instead. The stock, which closed near $158 on Thursday and is down about 54% over the past 12 months, slipped a further 3% to 5% in after-hours trading. Coinbase projected fourth-quarter subscription and services revenue of $550 million to $630 million, and filings alongside the results showed plans by senior insiders, including chief executive Brian Armstrong, to sell up to 13.6 million shares over the next 14 months — about 6% of the Class A shares, worth roughly $2.2 billion at Thursday's close.
